**SHIP-65 has left this table.** Its *Done when* — "returns full job including budget" — was met
but for the budget for two waves, and SHIP-67 closed it with the column and the proof together.
§10's note that a ticket can be both done and partly done still stands. **SHIP-118 left this table at
wave 9**, closed by SHIP-123 exactly as SHIP-65 was closed by SHIP-67.

**The live rows are now six — SHIP-158, SHIP-77, SHIP-102, SHIP-139, SHIP-143 and SHIP-79a — and
the sentence that counted them was wrong when this pass arrived**, which is the third time and is
becoming the point of the sentence rather than an aside. It read *"the live rows are now three —
SHIP-77, SHIP-151 and SHIP-102"*. Wave 11 struck SHIP-151 and added SHIP-158, so the **count** stayed
right by coincidence while the **names** went wrong, which is worse than an obviously stale number
because it survives a glance. §10's parallel sentence was wrong in the same way and is corrected in
the same pass. **A table read by a human and a sentence counting its rows are a semantic pair no
merge tool and no gate checks** — §7c's second merge finding, now demonstrated a third time.

**Four rows were added at this pass and three of them are the same shape as SHIP-118's.** SHIP-139
and SHIP-143 owe their missing half to **X-10**, written into `Docs/09` here; SHIP-102's owner
SHIP-79a landed and closed only the half it could. **SHIP-79a's own row is the fourth**, and it is
the first entry in this table whose missing half is a *second reader of something already built*
rather than a thing that does not exist.

**None of the four describes work a wave-12 lane is holding**, and that was checked ticket by ticket
against the dispatch rather than assumed: the two Firebase rows are external, SHIP-102's remaining
half is two fields on a Flutter comparison screen no lane has opened, and SHIP-79a's is an
administrative read and a feed disclosure that neither Lane A's verification work nor anything else
in flight touches. **A §4 row describing a gap a concurrent lane is closing is accurate when it is
written and stale when it is committed**, which is what bought wave 11 its only non-mechanical
conflict.

**SHIP-149 left it in the same wave**, closed by SHIP-150 building the write helper it had always
named — so wave 9 struck two of this table's four entries and added one. That the sentence above
needed correcting at the merge is itself the point: SHIP-123 struck SHIP-118 on one branch while
SHIP-150 struck SHIP-149 on another, neither could see the other, and **git auto-merged both without
a conflict**. A table read by a human and a sentence counting its live rows are a semantic pair no
merge tool checks.

**SHIP-118 has left this table, and it left the way this shape is supposed to end.** Its missing half
had an *owner* rather than being work that did not exist — SHIP-123, whose *Done when* names the two
fields and which depended on SHIP-118 directly — so the gap sat here as documentation ahead of code
rather than in §9 as a recommendation waiting on a ruling. Wave 9 built SHIP-123 and closed it:
`000607` adds both columns, required on `Delivered` and refused on every other milestone, in the
domain and in the schema. **`milestones.reason` was not reused for the delivery note**, as this row
insisted it should not be — it is the actor's optional note on any milestone, and a delivered row may
now carry both, meaning different things.

**SHIP-65 and SHIP-118 are now two worked examples of the same ending**, and they are worth reading
together by whoever next wants to put a row here: a missing half with a named owner closes, and a
missing half with none does not. SHIP-77 is the remaining example of the second kind.

**SHIP-77 is the SHIP-65 shape exactly, which is why it is here rather than being argued about.**
The screen landed, it is named by a commit subject, it is in `Docs/11-done.txt`, and one clause of
its *Done when* belongs to work that does not exist yet — an endpoint over `job_status_history`,
which no ticket in the backlog adds. The ticket did the honest thing with what it had: rather than
invent dates or tick steps a job may legitimately have skipped, the timeline says where the job is
and says out loud what it does not know. **It stays in the done list either way** — §10 explains
that removing it would hard-fail `make status` rather than making the record more truthful.

**SHIP-151 is the SHIP-118 shape rather than the SHIP-77 one, and as of this pass it has the owner
that shape needs.** SHIP-77's missing half belongs to work that does not exist — no ticket adds a
status-history endpoint — while SHIP-118's had an owner in SHIP-123 and closed. SHIP-151's had
**neither** for a wave: no ticket in `Docs/09` added a name to registration, and nothing else in the
platform wanted one. **It is now `Docs/09`'s SHIP-30a**, five points in M1, and the row costs the
milestone its completeness — M1 reads 28 of 29 — which is the honest price of writing the gap down
rather than leaving a shipped ticket permanently three terms out of four. This row stays here until
SHIP-30a lands.

**What it would cost, said plainly so the next reader does not re-derive it.** A `name` column on
`users`, collected at registration, is a migration in the **shared block (1–99)** — a *new* one, on
`000005_users_role_is_immutable`'s precedent, not an edit to `000002`, which is applied everywhere and
cannot be rewritten — plus `identity`'s register handler, its `User`, `userColumns`, and the mobile and
contract surfaces. A domain branch taking that unilaterally is the shared-surface edit the block rules
exist to prevent, which is why the row is written and not taken. Serving it once the column exists is
**one more `OR`** in `internal/admin/postgres_users.go` and one line in the contract. §6 struck
SHIP-169 for the same shared-block reason and this pass re-read that strike: it rests on a design
nobody has chosen, and if SHIP-169 does put its state on `users` then it wants the same migration slot
as SHIP-30a, which is an argument for taking the two together.

**The ticket is in the done list either way**, on §10's rule: three of four terms are demonstrable on
the wire, and removing the row would hard-fail `make status` rather than make the record more
truthful. **SHIP-30a does not change that** — it closes the fourth term, at which point this row
leaves §4 the way SHIP-65 and SHIP-118 did.

**SHIP-102 is the SHIP-118 shape, and the row is written here at the wave that landed it rather than
a wave later.** `Docs/09`'s SHIP-79a paragraph asked for exactly this — *"whoever reconciles the wave
that lands SHIP-102 should add it to `Docs/11` §4 with this row as its named owner"* — so this is the
mechanism closing on schedule rather than a gap discovered. Three of the four terms are served in
full and were re-checked against `routes_golden.txt` on `605ad3a` before this row was written: price
is `amount_cents`, timing is the two commitments, and the vehicle is `vehicle` with its declared
capability, all on line 46's `GET /v1/jobs/{id}/bids/received`. **The fourth is served in the only
form this platform stores**, and the screen says so on itself rather than implying it.

**What is missing is data, not presentation, which is why the owner is SHIP-79a and not a Flutter
row.** Measured on `605ad3a`: `internal/profiles` is `doc.go` and nothing else, eleven waves in;
`fleet.Profile` (`internal/fleet/model.go:437`) holds `ProviderID`, `Areas` and `Specialties`, and the
last two are precisely what SHIP-102a's *Done when* forbids disclosing to a customer, because they are
a competitor's map of the market. There is no trading name, no rating and no completed-job count in
any of the twenty-two tables. A screen can only render what exists, so SHIP-102 rendered the two facts
`users` can answer and named the absence out loud — which is the honest thing to do with what it had,
and is not the same as meeting the clause.

**One cross-reference in the code and in §3 points at the wrong ticket, and this pass corrects it
here rather than in either.** `internal/bidding/http.go`'s `offerResponse` comment and §3's SHIP-102a
and SHIP-102 entries all say the gap is closed by **SHIP-153…SHIP-159**. That was a reasonable reading
when it was written and it is now the weaker of the two answers: §6 strikes SHIP-153 in this pass as
*every dependency met and unbuildable in fact*, because `Docs/04` §4's five verification states exist
in no table at all — so the chain named as the closer is itself blocked on a prerequisite that had no
row until this pass wrote one. **SHIP-79a is the owner of this §4 row**; SHIP-79b and SHIP-153…159
would additionally give a customer a verification state richer than a boolean, which is a second
improvement rather than the one this clause needs. The code comment is left alone deliberately —
`internal/**` is not this branch's to edit and a comment that names a wave-late cross-reference is a
smaller defect than a prep branch reaching into a domain to fix it.

**This row was expected to leave §4 when SHIP-79a landed. SHIP-79a landed and it did not, and that
is the finding.** The prediction was the SHIP-65 → SHIP-67 and SHIP-118 → SHIP-123 pattern, and it
was made on a correct reading of where the gap was: *"what is missing is data, not presentation,
which is why the owner is SHIP-79a and not a Flutter row."* **The data arrived and the presentation
did not.** Measured on `5a3b8d7`: `internal/bidding/http.go` serves `display_name` and `operates_as`
on the offers endpoint, and `git grep` over `apps/mobile` for either spelling — snake case or camel
case — returns **nothing**. The screen still shows the two facts it showed in wave 10.

**Nobody did anything wrong, which is why this is worth a paragraph rather than a correction.**
SHIP-79a's *Done when* is about what the platform declares and discloses; it says nothing about a
Flutter screen, and the lane met it. SHIP-102 is in `Docs/11-done.txt` and stays there on §10's rule.
**What the pattern actually predicts is narrower than it was stated**: a §4 row with a named owner
closes when the owner's *Done when* covers the missing half, and closes only that far otherwise.
SHIP-118 → SHIP-123 worked because SHIP-123's *Done when* named the two fields. **A §4 row should
name the owner's clause, not just the owner.**

**What is left is small and has no owner at all**: two fields already on the wire, rendered on one
comparison screen. It is a Flutter row nobody has written, and it is the shape §9 keeps calling a
finding that goes quiet.

## 5. Blocked — and only by work outside this repository

**Track X is ten tickets now and one of them is closed.** X-6 was decided in wave 9 and is in the done list; the other nine have not started, none of them is code, and all of them are slow.

| Ticket | Gates |
|---|---|
| **X-1** D-U-N-S number | X-2, and through it SHIP-24, 25 |
| **X-2** Apple Developer Program | SHIP-24 (iOS signing), SHIP-25 (TestFlight) — and X-10's iOS leg, which needs an APNs key |
| **X-3** Google Play Console | SHIP-26 (Android signing), SHIP-27 (Play internal) |
| **X-4** Legal brief | X-7, X-8, X-9 — and SHIP-171, 172 |
| **X-5** Pilot metro area | Provider recruitment. No code |
| ~~**X-6**~~ Proof-exception auto-complete | **Closed** in wave 9 — the rule is in `Docs/02` §6.1. It gated SHIP-119, which shipped in the same wave |
| **X-7** Privacy policy URL | SHIP-180, 181 |
| **X-8** Terms and provider agreement | Pilot users |
| **X-9** Prohibited-goods list | SHIP-58 |
| **X-10** Firebase project and push credentials | **SHIP-144, SHIP-145** — and the unmet half of **SHIP-139** and **SHIP-143**, which are done in reduced form (§4) |

**X-1 → X-2 is the longest pole in the entire plan.** Apple's organisational enrolment commonly takes one to two weeks *after* a D-U-N-S number issues, and obtaining one that does not exist adds more. Every other M0 ticket proceeds without it, so starting costs nothing and waiting costs weeks of finished code with nowhere to put it.

X-5 needs no third party at all — it is a decision somebody can make this week. **X-10 is the same shape and is newer than the work behind it**: creating the Firebase project, downloading `google-services.json` and `GoogleService-Info.plist`, and issuing a service-account key need no approval from anybody. Only the iOS leg waits, on the APNs key that comes with X-2.

**X-10 is new at this pass, and the reason it took eleven waves is the most useful thing in this section.** **This table is the only place in the file that says "blocked by something outside the repository", and it is keyed on Track-X rows** — so work blocked on an external thing that *has no row* appears nowhere. Nothing created the Firebase project; SHIP-139 wrote the adapter against a fake FCM server and SHIP-143 shipped a `PushTokenSource` seam **with a test asserting the absence**, which is the honest form and is not the same as the thing existing. Both wrote it into §3, where it read as a note about one ticket rather than as a missing prerequisite for five. **SHIP-144 (2 points) and SHIP-145 (5) were startable on paper and not demonstrable in fact for two waves**, exactly as SHIP-153 was before the wave-10 pass wrote SHIP-81a.

**The test that would have caught it, stated so the next one is cheaper: for every external service in `Docs/06`'s stack table, name the Track-X row that procures it.** Datadog has none either — SHIP-174 is struck in §6 for exactly that, and the strike is doing the work an X row would do more honestly. AWS has none. The others are either local (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, MinIO) or already covered.

## 6. Ready to start now

Strict build order says the next ticket is the lowest-numbered open one, which is **SHIP-24** — and it is blocked on X-2, as are the other three M0 stragglers. **Twenty-two tickets have every dependency met: 17 code tickets worth 54 points, plus five Track-X tickets worth 12.** The lowest startable ticket of any kind is **X-1**; the lowest startable *code* ticket is **SHIP-65a**, which became startable when SHIP-83a landed. Build order is a preference rather than a constraint at this point.

**Two figures, and which one you want depends on what you are asking.** Measured on `develop` at `5a3b8d7` the set is **23 tickets and 70 points — 19 code at 61 plus four Track-X at 9**, which is the merged tree wave 12's lanes were dispatched against. Measured on this branch it is **22 and 66 — 17 code at 54 plus five Track-X at 12**, because this pass adds X-10 and gives SHIP-144 and SHIP-145 a dependency on it that takes both off the table. That is what a prep pass does to this table and the opposite of what a wave does; the whole-set figures below are this branch's.

**Every figure and every row was recomputed from `Docs/09`'s dependency column against `Docs/11-done.txt`** by a parser written for this pass, not adjusted from the last one and not taken from a dispatch brief. The parser was run against `5a3b8d7` first and reproduced `make status`'s done counts exactly before a single row was written, which is the only way to tell a correct figure from a copied one. It is the **complete** startable set; an early version of this table was a curated selection that read like a full list.

**Compute it from the dependency column and never from ticket order.** `Docs/09`'s header still warns of **ten forward edges across nine tickets**, and this pass added two more that are *not* forward — `SHIP-144 → X-10` and `SHIP-145 → X-10`, both backward, because Track X sorts first in build order. **The one forward edge that pointed at open work is satisfied**: `SHIP-65a → SHIP-83a` was the first in the file's history to name an unfinished target, SHIP-83a landed in wave 11, and SHIP-65a is on the table below as a result. The warning stays because the condition recurs the next time a lettered row is written ahead of its blocker.

**The set went from 30 to 23 across wave 11 and then to 22 on this branch, and the shrink is the thing to read.** Wave 11 closed **fourteen** rows off this table and opened **seven** — SHIP-65a (freed by SHIP-83a), SHIP-95a, SHIP-97, SHIP-121a, SHIP-131a, SHIP-144 and SHIP-145 — so the net movement is seven out. This is the first wave since the table was first written in which the startable set got **smaller by more than one**, and it is not because the board is nearly finished: it is because wave 11 closed four chains and the fan behind them is thin. What is left is dominated by rows the plan always intended to be last.

**Wave 12 is in flight as this is written, and it is holding ten of the seventeen code rows below.** Known from the dispatch rather than measured from the tree: **SHIP-78a and SHIP-81a** (Lane A), **SHIP-87a, SHIP-95a and SHIP-97** (Lane B), **SHIP-65a, SHIP-121a and SHIP-131a** (Lane C), **SHIP-147a and SHIP-147b** (Lane D), plus SHIP-81b, which is not on the table because SHIP-81a is its blocker. A reader picking this up mid-wave should not start what a lane is holding.

**Subtract the ten in flight and the five struck and the board has two rows left on it — SHIP-164 and SHIP-169.** That is worth stating plainly rather than leaving to arithmetic: **after wave 12 merges, the startable, sensible and unheld set is a dispute workflow and an account-deletion endpoint, five points and three.** Everything else needs either a wave-12 ticket to land first (SHIP-81b, SHIP-103, the SHIP-153 chain), an external row (X-1…X-5, X-7…X-10), or a decision this file has been carrying (§6's five strikes). **Whoever plans wave 13 is planning against a board that wave 12 very nearly empties**, and the two obvious answers are to schedule SHIP-164 — which was trimmed in wave 10 and has been the largest startable row ever since — and to take X-1 and X-10, neither of which needs an engineer at all.

**The startable-and-sensible set is 12 tickets and 37 points** — the 17 code tickets less the five struck. It was 24 and 72 a wave ago, on 30 code tickets less six struck, so **it has halved**, and the composition is what to read rather than the size: **ten of the twelve are held by a wave-12 lane**, and the two that are not are SHIP-164 and SHIP-169.

**Every strike below was re-read against today's code in this pass rather than carried**, which is what §6 exists to do: *a strike whose reason drifts while its verdict stays right is the failure this re-check catches.* **One no longer holds and has been removed; four were re-confirmed by measurement; one had its reason rewritten while its verdict stood; and one is half-answered by work in flight and was deliberately left alone.**

### SHIP-169's strike no longer holds, and it expired on the condition it wrote for itself

**The strike is removed and the reason is the one §6 named in advance.** A wave ago it read: *"if the
design puts deletion state on `users` it wants the shared migration block (1–99), and it would then
want the same slot as SHIP-30a — an argument for taking the two together rather than for striking
either… That opportunity closes the moment SHIP-30a lands alone."* **SHIP-30a landed alone in wave
11.** `services/core/migrations/000006_users_name.up.sql` is on `develop`, it was taken by the
identity lane, and no deletion column went with it. So the co-scheduling argument is spent, and it was
the only part of the entry that argued for a strike at all — **the sentence's own conclusion was
"rather than for striking either", which the table row had been contradicting for three waves.**

**What is left is a scheduling constraint, and a scheduling constraint is not a strike.** If the
design puts deletion state on `users` it wants a new shared-block migration on `000005`'s and
`000006`'s precedent, which is a shared surface a domain branch may not take unilaterally — the same
condition SHIP-30a met by being granted it. That is a sentence in a dispatch, not a reason a ticket
cannot be built.

**The design is also more settled than the strike implied, and this was measured rather than
assumed.** `Docs/05` §3.1 carries an **adopted** model, not an open question: the person is deleted
and the transaction is retained under a stable pseudonym, deletion is confirmed in-app and executed
within 30 days, a request during an active job is deferred rather than refused, and ordinary
administrators cannot execute one. `Docs/10` §3.3 forbids soft deletes for exactly that reason.
SHIP-169's *Done when* — *"a signed-in user can request deletion and receives a completion date"* —
has its completion date in §3.1 already.

**One caveat, named so nobody is surprised by it.** `Docs/05` §3.1's *Decision required* is the
retention period for pseudonymised records, owner legal, and it says *"needed before account deletion
is implemented"*. That binds **SHIP-171 and SHIP-172**, which §5 already lists behind X-4, and does not
bind the request endpoint or the deferral: the figure a user is told is thirty days, which is decided.
**SHIP-169 and SHIP-170 are startable; SHIP-171 and SHIP-172 are not**, and the row that says so is
X-4 rather than this section.

**It is 3 points and it stands in front of 16.** SHIP-170, 171, 172 and 173 all sit behind SHIP-169,
so this is the largest single fan on the board behind one open row, and it has been struck for three
waves on an argument its own prose disowned.

### SHIP-102's strike expired exactly as §6 predicted, and has been removed

**The condition §6 set a wave ago was exact and mechanical** — *"a `GET` collection of a job's bids appearing in `routes_golden.txt`"* — and it was met: `GET /v1/jobs/{id}/bids/received` is **line 46** of `routes_golden.txt` at `605ad3a`. SHIP-102a and SHIP-102 landed on one branch in wave 10, price, timing and vehicle are served in full, and the ticket is in `Docs/11-done.txt`. **§6 warned in writing not to carry this strike without re-reading the golden file, and the file was re-read before the strike was removed.**

**It is the fourth instance of "every dependency met and unbuildable in fact" to close properly** — after SHIP-114, SHIP-101 and SHIP-129's chain — and the first to close on a date the category itself named in advance. What SHIP-102 did *not* close is now §4's business rather than this section's: the provider-profile clause shipped in reduced form and SHIP-79a owns it.

### SHIP-153 is the same category and has left this table by a different door

**Measured on `605ad3a`, and every claim here is a count rather than an impression.** SHIP-153's *Done when* is *"pending provider verifications listed oldest first"*, and **there is no pending provider verification anywhere in this system**. `Docs/04` §4's five outcomes — Pending, Verified, Restricted, Rejected, Suspended — appear in **no table**: the schema holds twenty-two `CREATE TABLE` statements and not one of them records a verification; **migration block 200–299 is entirely unused**, the only empty block in the file; and `internal/profiles` has held `doc.go` and nothing else since SHIP-10 created it, eleven waves ago. `users.status` is a different question with three values — `active`, `restricted`, `suspended` — and `000002_users.up.sql` says so in its own column comment: *"Provider verification state is separate and lives with profiles (Docs/04 §4)."* `internal/fleet/eligibility.go` says the same thing at length, calls its own verification clause *"deliberately incomplete"*, and names the ticket it expected to complete it: *"The document-review half of Docs/04 §3 — licence, registration, insurance, ABN — arrives with SHIP-152…154."* **SHIP-152 shipped in wave 10 and is job and bid search. It built none of this**, correctly, because nothing in its *Done when* asks for it.

**The blast radius is four rows and 14 points**: SHIP-153 (3) blocks SHIP-154 (5), which blocks SHIP-155 (3) and SHIP-159 (3). Every one of them had every dependency met.

**This pass added the missing edge rather than keeping the strike, and that is a deliberate departure from the position §6 has held for four waves.** That position is worth restating before departing from it: *adding the missing edge to `Docs/09` would delete the category — a ticket whose prerequisite is declared is simply not startable, drops off this table, and the reader never learns that its dependencies are met and its data source is missing.* **The position is right about the cases it was written for and this is not one of them.** SHIP-114, SHIP-101, SHIP-102 and the three lettered read tickets were all cases where the *data existed* and no route served it — "practical buildability, which the dependency column does not record", as §6 puts it, and a route is not something `Docs/09` has ever expressed. SHIP-153's prerequisite is **not a route. It is a table, and a table is exactly what the dependency column is for**: `Docs/09`'s own header defines a dependency as what must be **built** before a ticket. So the honest fix was to write the row that builds it — `Docs/09`'s new **SHIP-81a**, five points in M3 — and give SHIP-153 a real edge to it.

**The category is preserved by this paragraph rather than by the strike, and that trade is the point.** SHIP-153 is no longer in the table above, because it is genuinely not startable; a reader who wants to know why finds it here. **The test for which treatment a case wants: can the missing thing be a row in `Docs/09` at all?** If yes, write the row and declare the edge. If it is a route, a served surface or a practical buildability the file has no vocabulary for, strike it and say what would lift the strike.

### SHIP-156 keeps its strike, and the asymmetry with SHIP-153 is the reasoning

**Re-measured on `5a3b8d7` rather than carried.** SHIP-156's *Done when* is *"reports surface with the job and conversation in context"*, and **neither half exists on the merged tree**. There is **no report or flag mechanism anywhere** — `grep -iE 'create table[^;]*\b(report|reports|flag|flags|moderation)'` over every migration returns nothing, against a schema that now holds **twenty-five** `CREATE TABLE` statements rather than twenty-two, so three tables arrived in wave 11 and none of them is this. And there is **no conversation**: no migration creates a message, thread or conversation table either.

**Half of it is being built as this is written, and the strike is deliberately left in place.** SHIP-97 — job-scoped messaging — is **Lane B in wave 12**. When it lands, the conversation half of SHIP-156 exists and the report half still does not. **A strike must not be lifted on the strength of a branch that has not merged**, which is the wishful entry §10 warns about, and it must not be lifted on half a *Done when* either. **Whoever merges wave 12 owns this row**: re-read it against the merged tree, and if SHIP-97 landed, rewrite the strike so it rests on the report mechanism alone rather than on both halves.

**Why it is struck rather than given a dependency edge, which is the reasoning that survives either way.** SHIP-156's conversation half *does* have a row — SHIP-97 — and declaring that edge alone would take SHIP-156 off this table while leaving the larger half, the report mechanism, owned by nothing. **A half-declared dependency is worse than none**: it makes the ticket look blocked on a scheduling problem when it is blocked on a product decision nobody has taken. What is reportable, by whom, with what outcome and against what policy is `Docs/04` §5's territory and is not a row a reconciliation pass may invent. **What would lift the strike is named: a `Docs/09` row for the report mechanism, plus SHIP-97.** §9 carries the item for whoever writes the next prep, and it is the third consecutive pass to carry it.

### SHIP-174, SHIP-178 and SHIP-182 — re-confirmed, and one reason needed tightening

**All three verdicts hold and every one was re-measured on `5a3b8d7` rather than carried.** `deploy/docker-compose.yml` declares four services — `postgres`, `redis`, `kafka`, `minio` — and none is an agent. There is **no `DD_*` variable anywhere in the repository**. `git grep -niE 'sentry|crashlytics|bugsnag'` returns nothing **repository-wide**, which is stronger than the `apps/mobile`-only claim the last two passes made and is worth stating in the stronger form because it closes the "maybe it is wired somewhere else" reading. `git grep -E 'pg_dump|pg_restore'` returns exactly **one** match in the whole repository, and it is this section's own SHIP-182 row describing the strike.

**The Datadog reason needed correcting a second time, in the same direction, and that is worth more than the correction.** The wave-10 pass fixed *"every occurrence outside the documents is a comment"* to *"seven occurrences, two of them not comments"*. Re-measured here: **seven occurrences outside `Docs/` is still right, and three of them are not comments** — `CLAUDE.md`'s stack table, `Source/Shipper.md`'s, and `contracts/components/schemas/error.yaml:60`, which is a `description:` block in the **published contract** rather than a code comment. So the claim has now been slightly too strong twice, corrected twice, and slightly too strong again. **The verdict is untouched and was never in doubt** — naming a vendor in a stack table or a schema description is not an agent ingesting traces — but a reason that keeps needing the same correction is a reason nobody should restate without re-running the grep.

**What SHIP-174 does not have and probably should is a Track-X row.** Datadog is a purchased external service with an account, an API key and a bill, exactly like the Apple and Google enrolments X-2 and X-3 exist for, and **no row in `Docs/09` procures it** — which is the same shape as the Firebase project X-10 was written for at this pass. It is left as a strike rather than made a row, because unlike the Firebase project nothing is *shipping* against its absence: SHIP-174 and its four dependants are the only work involved and all five are struck or blocked behind it. **§5 names the general test** — for every external service in `Docs/06`'s stack table, name the row that procures it — and this is the second entry that test finds.

### SHIP-183 keeps its strike and its reason is rewritten

**The verdict stands and the reason it was given for does not, which is precisely what this re-read exists to catch.** §6 has recorded SHIP-183 for several waves as *"a decision ticket — §9 parks the per-account-lockout question here"*. **That is circular.** SHIP-183 is where the decision is taken; a ticket cannot be blocked on its own output, and reading it that way is how a row stays struck for ever.

**The load-bearing half is the other clause: it rewrites limits on every domain's routes.** Measured on `5a3b8d7`: the manifest holds **70 routes**, and `ratelimit.New` is constructed at exactly **two** sites — `cmd/api/routes_identity.go:173` and `cmd/api/routes_admin.go:357` — both sign-in shaped, each with an account bucket and an address bucket. So sixty-odd routes have no considered limit, and giving them one is a change spanning every domain's route file at once. **That is a whole-wave or owner-serialised ticket rather than a lane ticket**, which is a real reason a lane should not pick it up and a completely different reason from the one this entry has been giving.

**It is getting larger while it waits, and the measurement is now two waves deep.** Wave 10 added thirteen administrative routes; wave 11 added seven routes of which four are administrative, taking `/v1/admin/` from 13 to **17**. An administrative route is the one place where a per-account lockout somebody else can trigger is most damaging, and none of the seventeen has a limit.

### The three lettered read tickets still appear in no `Depends on` cell, and SHIP-102a is now four

**Re-measured on this branch**: SHIP-101a, SHIP-115a, SHIP-120a, SHIP-102a and now SHIP-96a and SHIP-79a are named by no other row's dependency column. What they supplied was **practical buildability, which the dependency column does not record** — and SHIP-102a is the worked proof of it, because SHIP-102 depended on SHIP-77 and SHIP-96 and on neither of the two things it actually needed. **SHIP-121a is written the same way** and SHIP-65a is the exception, because there the missing thing was a router constraint rather than a route, and a router constraint *is* expressible as an edge — which SHIP-65a declared to SHIP-83a and which wave 11 satisfied.

**X-10 is the first row this file has written that closes the gap from the other end, and that is the addition worth carrying.** The category has always been "a route the dependency column cannot express". **A procured external service is a different thing entirely, and it *is* expressible** — Track X exists for exactly it, X-2 and X-3 are the precedent, and `SHIP-144 → X-10` is an ordinary backward edge that makes a ticket stop reading as startable. **So the test is now three-way rather than two-way**, and it is the one to apply to the next ticket that looks startable and is not: can the missing thing be a `Docs/09` row? If it is a *table*, write the row and declare the edge (SHIP-81a). If it is an *external account or credential*, write a Track-X row and declare the edge (X-10). If it is a *route on the served surface*, the file has no vocabulary for it — strike the ticket and say what would lift the strike.

**Public routes still share the anonymous idempotency scope, and that remains safe** for the reason §6 has given since SHIP-44: `replayOrRefuse` fingerprints method, path and body, so reading another caller's stored response requires sending their exact request — which, on every route on `Docs/10` §4.1's allow-list, means already holding the secret material in their body. **What is new is that administrators share it too**, which nobody had noticed until a wave-10 lane watched a key collide. It is the same posture and not a new hole, and it is a weaker property than SHIP-44 established for users on the most privileged surface there is. `Docs/09`'s new **SHIP-147b** owns it.

### Two findings worth more than the tickets

**A required field on registration broke 37 `make verify` call sites across nine sections, and no
unit test could have shown it.** SHIP-30a made `name` required by `POST /v1/auth/register`, and every
verify section that registers an account carries **its own JSON literal** — there is no shared
"register a user" helper anywhere in `scripts/verify/`. The domain tests were green throughout,
because a domain test constructs its own request. §9 carries the item: the harness has a shared
`ticket`, `ok`, `fail`, `json`, `post_json` and token minting, and no shared account fixture, so the
next required registration field costs the same 37 edits.

**`Docs/02` §2 has no `Awarded → Cancelled` transition, so SHIP-158's obvious implementation is
*inverted* rather than incomplete.** A post-award cancellation queue keyed on a job reaching
`Cancelled` returns the *pre*-award cancellations and none of the post-award ones — the exact inverse
of what the row asks for. The lane read `job_status_history` instead, on two outcomes, and was right
to; what it could not do from a lane branch is settle whether `Docs/02` §2 is missing a row or whether
the platform is missing a transition. §9 has it, and it is a document decision before it is a code
one.

| `9e4c580` | `ship-15u-wave-10-prep` | `3e5b817` | 697 / 15 | 697 / 15 |
| `178e44d` | `ship-138-140-notifications-dispatch` | `cbb9380` | 712 / 15 | 712 / 15 |
| `4fefef8` | `ship-70a-128-jobs-and-delivery` | `c2528f0` | 714 / 15 | 714 / 15 |
| `711e25a` | `ship-102a-102-customer-offers` | `83c5c26` | 704 / 15 | 714 / 15 |
| `605ad3a` | `ship-152-165-admin-breadth` | `549c4f8` | 747 / 15 | **747 / 15** |

**Both columns were read off the tree at each ref with `git show <ref>:Docs/11-delivery-status.md`**,
not taken from anybody's report. Read the last two rows together. At `711e25a` the resolution kept
`develop`'s 714 over the branch's 704; at `605ad3a` it kept the branch's 747 over `develop`'s 714.
**Each resolution chose a side, and choosing a side is precisely what `Docs/10` §9.2's recipe for this
line forbids** — *"never take a side; both are usually wrong. Re-run `make verify` on the merged tree
— it fails with the true figure — then `make verify-update`."*

**So `develop` at `605ad3a` publishes a check count that is one branch's own figure rather than the
merged tree's**, which is the failure wave 3 recorded, wave 5 paid for with
`ship-15j-wave-5-merge-repair`, and nine consecutive waves have demonstrated: **the merged figure is
never any branch's own.** It cost nothing this time because nothing reads the number except the guard
that checks it, and the guard's response to a wrong number is to fail the next run with the right one.
It is written up here because the failure is a *process* one — the wave ended without anybody running
`make verify` on the merged tree at all — and a wave that skips the last gate will eventually skip one
that matters.

### What the wave built

**M5 stopped being a consumer with nothing to send.** SHIP-137's consumer had run since wave 9 with no
transport behind it; SHIP-138 gave it email templates and dispatch, SHIP-139 wrote the Firebase
adapter into `internal/platform/push` — **the last of the five adapters still holding `doc.go`
alone** — and SHIP-140 put a device token behind it. Every adapter directory under
`internal/platform/` now holds code.

**M6 went from two product reads to seven.** SHIP-152 searches jobs and bids, SHIP-160 unpublishes,
SHIP-161 restricts or suspends, SHIP-162 attaches internal notes and SHIP-165 serves the audit log
back — all over SHIP-150's audit writer, so every one of them leaves a trail. `routes_golden.txt`
holds **13 lines under `/v1/admin/`** at `605ad3a`, up from 4.

**M3's customer half reached the thing the marketplace is for.** SHIP-102a serves a job's offers to
its owning customer and SHIP-102 is the comparison over it — the pair §6 had struck for two waves as
*every dependency met and unbuildable in fact*, taken on one branch, which is the right answer to a
read-and-screen pair and the same call wave 8 made for SHIP-89 → SHIP-90. **§4 carries what the pair
did not close**: three of SHIP-102's four comparison terms are served in full and the provider profile
is served in the only form this platform stores.

**And SHIP-70a corrected a narrowing nobody had reopened a ticket for.** Both expiry sweeps claimed
`WHERE status = 'Open'`, which stopped being "a live job" the moment SHIP-90 introduced `Negotiating`;
`000409` widens the index and the claim together, and `Docs/02` §2's expiry row was widened first, as
the ticket's *Done when* required.

One pre-step serially, then four tracks concurrently. **Eleven tickets, thirty-seven points, all

| **Autocomplete and consumer** | SHIP-119, 137 | Both, 8 points — and **the only branch in the wave to add a verify section**, two of them |
| **Admin audit and search** | SHIP-150, 151 | Both, 8 points — M6's first product reads |
| **Driver portal arc** | SHIP-121 → 122 → 123 | All three, 11 points — a strict three-deep chain bought whole |

**Every figure above was measured on this tree rather than carried from a dispatch brief.** The
ticket set is the difference between `Docs/11-done.txt` at `ac62673` (136 declared, 414 points) and
at `360da43` (147, 451); the branch attributions are the same difference taken per branch tip. Wave
1 delivered 32 points, wave 2 37, wave 3 48, wave 4 39, wave 5 37, wave 6 47, wave 7 49, wave 8 49,
and wave 9 **37 across four tracks** — the first fall in three waves, and the composition explains it
rather than the concurrency: one track spent 11 of its points on a chain that cannot be split, and
the wave carried no five-point platform ticket at all.

### The chain was the wave, and buying it whole was the right call

**SHIP-121 → 122 → 123 is three deep and could not be split across tracks.** §6 said so a wave
early — "a wave that wants the driver portal finished is buying a chain, not three rows" — and the
wave bought it. The result is the fourth deployable finished: a driver opens a link, records every
milestone from a phone browser, photographs the delivery straight into the object store through a
pre-signed URL the API is not in the path of, names who took it and what was left where, and finds
the page read-only afterwards.

**Its cost is visible in the points total and was correctly priced in advance**, which is the part
worth keeping. A three-deep chain in a four-track wave spends one track's whole capacity on three
rows; wave 7 ran two four-deep chains for the same reason and landed 49 because the other two tracks
carried breadth. Wave 9's other three tracks carried five tickets between them.

### `make verify` went 642 → 664 → 678 → 697 → 697, and only the last figure is any branch's business

| Merge | Branch | Tip | Its own §3 figure | The figure after the merge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `9a5fc4e` | `ship-15t-wave-9-prep` | `7d7caf0` | 642 / 13 | 642 / 13 |
| `f860f19` | `ship-119-137-autocomplete-and-consumer` | `d4e859e` | 664 / 15 | 664 / 15 |
| `abfec71` | `ship-150-151-admin-audit-and-search` | `3235c73` | 656 / 13 | 678 / 15 |
| `f64eba1` | `ship-121-123-driver-portal-arc` | `4e4364f` | 661 / 13 | 697 / 15 |
| `360da43` | `ship-101-133-flutter-client-reads` | `388679f` | 600 / 13 | 697 / 15 |

**Both columns were read off the tree at each ref rather than taken from anybody's report**, with
`git show <ref>:Docs/11-delivery-status.md`. **The merged answer of 697 is no branch's own figure**,
which is the sixth consecutive wave in which the last number in this table is one nobody could have
written down in advance — and it is the argument for measuring the line on the merged tree instead of
reconciling it, which has been the rule since wave 3.

**One qualification, because the general claim is usually made a little too strongly.** The *first*
track merge did land on its own branch's figure, and had to: `ship-119-137` was cut from the pre-step
and merged straight onto it, so nothing else had moved the count. The claim that holds every time is
about the **final** figure, not each intermediate one.

**The 600 in the last row is the finding.** `ship-101-133-flutter-client-reads` was cut from
`ac62673` rather than from the pre-step — `git merge-base` against `7d7caf0` returns `ac62673`, while
the other three return `7d7caf0` — so it carried `develop`'s stale wave-8 figure the whole way and
its §3 line disagreed with the merged tree by 97. It cost nothing, because the line is measured
rather than reconciled. **It would have cost a great deal if anybody had resolved that conflict by
choosing a side**, which is exactly the failure wave 3 recorded and the reason the rule exists.

**Wave 10 measured the thing wave 7 inferred, and the answer is that the base a branch is cut from is
not what prevents a conflict — writing the same section is what causes one.** Wave 7 concluded that
cutting every track from the pre-step "removes the conflict wave 6 paid four times", and wave 9
followed it three times in four. **Measured across wave 10's five branches with `git merge-tree
--write-tree --name-only`, every branch cut from the same `develop` commit**: all six pairs among the
four *lanes* conflict, every one of them in `Docs/11-delivery-status.md`, because every lane appends
to §3 and §3 is deliberately not `merge=union`. Three of the four are **clean against the prep
branch**, which touched every section of that file except §3.

**The fourth is the evidence, and it is the prep branch's own doing.** `ship-15u-wave-10-prep`
conflicts with exactly one lane, in exactly one hunk, and the hunk is a **single token** the prep
changed inside §3 — the X-6 summary row's cross-reference — sitting immediately below three rows that
lane appended to the same table. **One line in a section it did not own bought the only collision it
had.** Cutting from the pre-step was never the mechanism; it correlated with it, because a branch cut
from prep is usually a branch that has not written prose into the shared narrative. **Section
ownership is the mechanism**, and it is cheaper than re-basing a wave, because it is a rule about
what a branch may write rather than about when it may start.

### Three merge findings, and they are worth more than the tickets

Four conflicts across the wave, all in this file. The three below are recorded at length because each
one is a *class* rather than an incident. **The branch and ticket attributions were re-derived from
`Docs/11-done.txt` and from §4's own text; the line counts are as the merge session reported them and
were not re-measured here.**

**One. Two of the four conflicts were not unions, and a union would have been wrong.** §4's SHIP-118
row was live on `HEAD` — "no column holds either" — and **struck** on the driver-portal branch,
because SHIP-123's `000607` added exactly those two columns. A union appends both sides, so the file
would have asserted the gap and its closure in consecutive rows. This section has said "both
resolutions were unions" often enough for it to read as the default; it is not the default, and a
union is only ever right for a flat list of independent tokens.

**Two. A table and a sentence counting its rows are a semantic pair no merge tool checks.** The
driver-portal branch struck §4's SHIP-118 row while the admin branch struck SHIP-149 in the same
wave, neither could see the other, and the sentence beneath the table — *"SHIP-77 and SHIP-149 are the
live examples"* — was written on one branch and invalidated on the other. **They are different lines,
so git auto-merged both with no conflict at all** and produced a clean-looking file with a false
statement in it. The correction is in §4 now. There is no mechanical fix available: `make status`
checks that every done ticket **has** a §3 row and cannot see what a sentence claims about a table.

**Three. The resolution error, which is the most useful of the three.** A first attempt at one
conflict located the check-count sentence by matching the string `"checks across"` — which also
appears **inside §3's prose narratives**, a dozen times over. The match landed on a 711-line prose
hunk, the resolution kept `HEAD`, and **380 lines of one branch's §3 entries were silently
discarded**. Zero conflict markers remained. The file looked clean, `make check` was green, and
nothing in the repository could have told anybody.

**It was caught by counting what had to be there — eight §3 headings present where eleven were
required — and not by looking for what should not be.** That is the rule, and it generalises past
this file: **verify a resolution against what must be present, never against what is absent.** The
absence of conflict markers is evidence that a resolution *completed*, not that it was correct, and
in this instance the two were opposite. The cheap instrument for this file is the one that found it:
count the §3 headings against the tickets the wave declared, before running any gate.

### The consumer fence held, and the harness is still not concurrency-safe

`ship-15t` fenced `kafka_consume_fenced` on run-start offsets, which is what let `make verify` reach
`90-admin.sh` again after `shipper.bid` outgrew the old consumer's window. **Two tracks then found,
independently and by id rather than by timing, that the fence is necessary and not sufficient**: one
saw five extra ids on `shipper.job` that `select id from outbox where id in (…)` against its own
database did not claim, with `ps` showing two other harnesses live; the other saw a
`job.status_changed` carrying section 80's own marker reason for an aggregate absent from its own
database, while its own event was nowhere on the topic. §9 has the two failure modes and why only one
of them is a fencing problem. The operational half is now a row in `CLAUDE.md`'s worktree table; the
assertion half is `Docs/09`'s SHIP-134a.

### The two tickets nobody had ever been the wave for

**SHIP-56a had been cut six times and SHIP-136 three.** §6 has said for two waves that a deferral with
no reason written down is how a ticket goes quiet, and named those two as the worked examples. Both
are built. SHIP-56a is the more interesting of the pair, because its cost was never the work — the
ticket writes into `services/core`, `apps/mobile` and `apps/driver-portal` at once, so under
contention it lost to every ticket that opened one tree. **It wanted a serial slot and it eventually
got one**, cut from the pre-step rather than from `develop`.

SHIP-136 wanted the opposite: three domain packages free at the same time. Wave 8 was the first wave
whose composition allowed it, exactly as §6 predicted a wave earlier — its client tickets opened no Go
package, so `jobs`, `bidding` and `delivery` were free for the whole of it.

### `develop` was red on `make verify` when the wave closed, and no gate said so

The wave landed with `Docs/11` §3 stating **600 checks** against a true **642**. `make verify` fails on
that disagreement by design (SHIP-15i), so `develop` exited 2 on that gate from the moment the last
branch merged until SHIP-15t measured it.

**Every branch figure in circulation was wrong, and each was right about its own branch.** 555, 560,
570, 575, 600 and "~620" were all published during the wave; SHIP-15r's §3 entry states 560 as an
absolute from 555 and SHIP-136's states 570 the same way — both true of their own branch, and **only
the first to land reads true on `develop`**. Nothing reads those figures, which is why they survived.
They are corrected in §3 to name the branch each was measured on.

**And the gate could not have told anybody, because it never ran to the end.** `shipper.bid` had
reached 1582 messages, past the old consumer's five-hundred-message window, so section 80 failed on
every tree and section 90 never ran at all. Three lanes hit it independently and each read it as a
flake. That is SHIP-15t's first item, and §3 has the account.

### Two clocks, twice, in two lanes that never spoke

Track C's `admin_sessions.created_at` takes `DEFAULT now()` while its expiries are computed from the
injected Go clock; Track B's sync harness was pinned to a fixed date while the nudge read the host
clock. **Neither is a flake.** The first passes for one idle window and then fails for ever, and the
second was measuring the calendar. §9 carries it as a class — *a row whose timestamps come from two
clocks is a test that expires* — because two independent instances in one wave is a pattern rather
than an accident.

### What the wave cost in scale

Wave 1 delivered 32 points, wave 2 delivered 37, wave 3 delivered 48, wave 4 delivered 39, wave 5
delivered 37, wave 6 delivered 47, wave 7 delivered 49, and wave 8 delivered **49 across five
branches** — level with wave 7 on points and **ahead of it by one ticket at fifteen**. Eight waves have
now settled the concurrency question: the point total moves with the composition rather than with the
number of tracks, and five branches produced exactly what four did.

What changed is the **shape**. Wave 7 ran two four-deep chains and wave 8 ran none longer than three,
so one more branch bought no more points. A chain cannot be split across tracks, and a wave of short
chains spends its concurrency on breadth instead.

## 7d. Wave 7 — what landed

One ticket serially, then four tracks concurrently. **Fourteen tickets, forty-nine points, all
delivered, no trim taken.**

| Step | Tickets | Landed |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-step** (serial, primary tree) | SHIP-15p | Merged at `c20c126` before any track started |
| **Track A** the award transaction | SHIP-92 → 93 → 94 → 95 | All four, 16 points — three sequential runs on one branch, **the third written adversarially** |
| **Track B** proof and storage | SHIP-114 → 115 → 116 → 118 | All four, 14 points — four sequential runs, the wave's longest chain |
| **Track C** provider client | SHIP-100, 126, 129, 168 | All four, 11 points — three runs |
| **Track D** driver portal | SHIP-120 | 5 points — two runs, the second closing the two gaps the first recorded |

**Thirteen agent runs**, and the exit criterion was: a customer can award one offer and only one,
under the lock ordering SHIP-88 wrote down, with the races observed rather than assumed; a
photograph reaches an object store this API is not in the path of, becomes evidence for one recorded
milestone, and a delivery that could not be photographed has something to say instead; `Delivered`
becomes recordable and is refused when it carries neither; the driver's link opens a page that shows
one job and no other; and the provider's half of the app can place a bid and record a milestone
through the durable queue. **All of it holds**, and `make verify` went from 481 checks across 13
sections to 555 across the same 13. `make flutter-check` went from 594 host tests to 766, and
`make web-check` went from **0 tests to 25** — not because the driver portal had none, but because
`web-check` never ran the suite until this wave wired `web-test` into it between the lint and the
build.

### The two things the wave existed to do, both closed, and both proved rather than asserted

**The award transaction, out of reach for three waves.** SHIP-92's second dependency was SHIP-88,
which sat four hops behind the provider feed, and §8 has carried "SHIP-92…95 never parallelise" since
SHIP-15a wrote this file in wave 1. It is built: one offer accepted and the job moved in one
transaction, against the lock
ordering §3's SHIP-88 entry recorded rather than one invented on the branch, idempotent by **state**
so it needed no key column and no migration. What makes it more than a claim is SHIP-95 — `Docs/08`'s
four named races, each one *observed* by holding a transaction open and polling `pg_blocking_pids`
until PostgreSQL confirms the other backend is waiting, rather than released together and hoped for.

**"Delivered requires photo proof or a recorded exception reason, never neither."** `CLAUDE.md` has
listed that as an invariant since before any of the machinery existed, and `Docs/02` §3's own line
had no enforcement behind it since the status model was written — because `Delivered` was a status
nothing could reach. It is now enforced in the domain, where a client gets `409
delivery_proof_required` and is told which of the two to send, and again by a
`DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` constraint trigger that refuses the row at `COMMIT` whoever wrote it.
**Deferred is load-bearing rather than tidy**: the evidence points at the milestone and can only be
written second, so an ordinary `AFTER INSERT` trigger refuses every honest delivery there is — making
it `NOT DEFERRABLE` fails nine tests. And the second layer is demonstrated the only way a second
layer can be: a **raw SQL insert that bypasses the service entirely** is refused, in the domain's
tests and again in `make verify`.

### Cutting every track from the prep branch removed the conflict wave 6 paid four times

§7e records this as the cheapest process change available, found by accident on a single track.
Wave 7 applied it deliberately to all four, and the result is measurable: **all four branches merged
clean against `ship-15p`.** Wave 6's three tracks that were cut from `develop` while the previous
reconciliation sat unmerged each met it in this file, and the one cut from the pre-step did not.

What remained was smaller and is worth naming precisely, because it is what the rule does not fix.
**One pair met each other**: the Flutter track and the driver-portal track both wrote §3 prose, and
two tracks appending to §3 is the conflict this file will always have. And **the proof branch met the
other three at the end**, being the last of the four to merge — which is the ordinary last-merge cost
that §7i recorded in wave 2 and which no ordering decision removes. The mechanism only removes the
conflict with the *reconciliation*; it does not remove the tracks' conflict with each other.

### The adversarial run earned its place, and the argument is now evidence rather than a recommendation

§8 asked for this for six waves — "consider using a second agent adversarially — one implements
92–94, another writes SHIP-95 from `Docs/02` §3 and `Docs/08`'s four named races *without reading the
implementation*". Wave 7 did it, and the arrangement is no longer a suggestion.

**What "blind" meant, exactly**, because a loose version of this would prove nothing: the author read
`Docs/02` §3, `Docs/08`'s four named races, `contracts/paths/bidding.yaml`, `errors.go`, `model.go`,
the fixtures, and the exported signatures through `go doc` — and did not open `service.go`,
`postgres.go`, `ports.go`, `http.go` or `cmd/api/routes_bidding.go`, nor any test whose name contains
"Award".

**It killed two of the three weaknesses SHIP-92 left, and established that the third was not a
weakness at all.** With `race_test.go` removed, the pre-existing package passes entirely under the
bid-before-job lock mutation, and passes under the both-guards-removed mutation except for a test
that fires about counters rather than about the award. No award test noticed either. The third
finding is the more interesting one: the accept's compare-and-set is **redundant**, because the award
decides liveness under the bid's own `FOR UPDATE`, so either guard alone suffices and **no suite can
distinguish removing one**. Remove both and the award succeeds on a withdrawn offer. Nothing was
changed — it is a note for whoever next edits `acceptBid` or `lockBid`, and it is the kind of finding
a suite written from the same reading as the code cannot produce, because it is a fact about the code
rather than about the specification.

### A report where every mutation was caught is the one to probe

§7e recorded this after wave 6 and wave 7 gives it more evidence, which is why it is restated rather
than referred to. **Four mutations survived across the whole wave, and every one of them produced a
real change:**

| What survived | What it produced |
|---|---|
| The driver portal deriving the job identifier from its own credential | A wire test that asks what path the process actually requested, rather than scanning source for a decode — because a scan is what §7e's budget guard was defeated by |
| A staleness guard whose own suite could not arrange the interleaving | `stale_snapshot_test.dart`, which arranges it — the guard stops a stale snapshot telling a driver with no signal that Shipper has their update |
| A missing `try`/`catch` | Its absence would have stopped the app drawing a frame at all, which no existing test reached |
| The award's redundant compare-and-set | The note above, and the black-box inference that the liveness decision is made under the bid's row lock |

**Two agents volunteered that their own clean sweeps were the weaker result**, unprompted, which is
the review posture this entry is arguing for rather than the finding itself. A mutation set that all
dies is either a tight suite or a set of mutations aimed where the tests already are, and from the
outside those look identical. The useful review question stays "which ones survived, and what did each
one reveal".

### `git checkout <file>` destroyed uncommitted work in two lanes

Two tracks lost work this way while reverting mutations, and it is worth naming because it is the
**obvious** revert and it is wrong on an unstaged tree: `git checkout <file>` restores the file from
the index, which discards every uncommitted change in it — including the ones that are not the
mutation. The mutation is deliberate and reversible; the hour of work sitting beside it in the same
file is neither.

The recipe both lanes converged on afterwards is in §3's mutation tables and belongs in `CLAUDE.md`
beside the existing mutation guidance: **copy the file aside or tar-snapshot the tree first, restore
from the copy, and confirm with `git diff` *and* a checksum.** The checksum is the part that is easy
to drop and is the reason the recipe works — `git diff` reporting nothing proves the file matches the
index, which is exactly what it did after the destructive revert too.

### What the wave cost in scale

Wave 1 delivered 32 points, wave 2 delivered 37, wave 3 delivered 48, wave 4 delivered 39, wave 5
delivered 37, wave 6 delivered 47, and wave 7 delivered **49 across four tracks** — **the largest by
points and the largest by ticket count at fourteen**, taking both records from wave 6 by two and one.
Seven waves have settled the concurrency question completely: four tracks is what works, and the
point total moves with the composition rather than with the effort.

What changed in wave 7 is that **two of the four tracks were four-deep chains at once**, where wave 6
had one five-deep chain and wave 5 had one four-deep. A chain cannot be split across tracks at all, so
two of them consumed half the wave's concurrency for its whole length — and the counterpart held as
well as it did in wave 6: six of the fourteen tickets closed were unblocked inside their own branch
and never appeared in §6 at all.

## 7e. Wave 6 — what landed

One ticket serially, then four tracks concurrently. **Thirteen tickets, forty-seven points, all
